title: Find the Longest Common DNA Subsequence
real_world_story: A biological research system compares DNA sequences from two samples to identify the longest sequence of genetic elements that appears in both samples while preserving their original order.

real_world_connection.system: DNA sequence comparison and biological analysis system
real_world_connection.input_represents: DNA sequences obtained from two biological samples
real_world_connection.target_represents: The longest sequence shared by both DNA samples
real_world_connection.algorithm_represents: Finding the longest common subsequence while preserving the order of biological sequence elements

problem_statement: Given two DNA sequences, find the length of their Longest Common Subsequence (LCS). A subsequence can be formed by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the remaining characters.
task: Compare the two DNA sequences and return the length of their longest common subsequence.
input_format: The first line contains the first DNA sequence. The second line contains the second DNA sequence.
output_format: Print a single integer representing the length of the Longest Common Subsequence.
constraints: DNA sequences contain only the characters A, C, G, and T

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is 'AGTAC', which has length 5.
The two DNA sequences share a longest common subsequence of length 20.

expected_algorithm.name: Longest Common Subsequence using Dynamic Programming
expected_algorithm.reason: DNA sequences may contain common genetic patterns at different positions, so dynamic programming can efficiently determine the longest sequence shared while preserving order.

hint: Create a table representing prefixes of the two DNA sequences.
If the current nucleotides match, extend the common subsequence.
Otherwise, consider skipping a nucleotide from either sequence and keep the larger result.
real_world_takeaway: LCS can help researchers compare biological sequences and identify shared genetic patterns even when insertions or deletions occur between matching elements.
